findings.title: Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous and renderer collide on UID 0
findings.body: The new denial-cache key is built from `checkReq.UserUID`, which for different identity types can be the same string. Anonymous subjects arrive as `anonymous:0` (UID `0`) and render-service subjects as `render:0` (UID `0`), so both produce the same key `namespace.perm_0_<action>_<name>_<parent>`. If an anonymous user is denied access to a dashboard (caching a denial under UID `0`), a renderer check for the same dashboard/action/folder within the 30s TTL takes the early `return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed:false}` at line 120 and is denied even though `getRendererPermissions` grants `*` for `dashboards:read`/`folders:read`. Consequence: image/PDF rendering intermittently fails to read dashboards whenever an anonymous denial was recently cached for the same resource. The key must include the identity type (and ideally use the resolved identity, not the raw subject UID).

findings.title: Denial cache is not invalidated on permission changes, re-introducing the creator-lockout in a race
findings.body: The denial is cached with `shortCacheTTL` (30s) and there is no hook to evict `permDenialCache` when permissions are granted (new dashboard/folder owned by creator, team/dashboard permission added, etc.). The PR's goal is to let a creator fetch a resource they just created; if the first `Check` for the new resource runs before the permission row is visible to `GetUserPermissions` (propagation/commit delay), that first check returns false and stores a denial keyed by the resource. The creator's retries are then served by the denial cache for up to 30s, so they still cannot access the newly created dashboard/folder during the window — the exact symptom being fixed. Consider invalidating denial entries on writes or using a much shorter TTL for denials of just-created resources.

findings.title: Denial-cache write path and cache-served denial are untested
findings.body: `TestService_CacheCheck`'s "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" seeds `permDenialCache` directly, so it only exercises the read path. Nothing verifies that a real denial (line 154 of service.go) writes to `permDenialCache`, nor that a second identical `Check` is subsequently answered from the denial cache without hitting the store (e.g., asserting `store.calls` stays constant on the second call). The new write path and the intended performance benefit are therefore unprotected against regressions.

findings.title: permissionCacheUsage conflates the denial cache with the permission cache
findings.body: The `permissionCacheUsage` metric is incremented on a denial-cache hit (line 118) as if it were a permission-cache hit, and on a permission-cache hit that ultimately denies the request it is recorded as `"false"` (line 137). Since the metric is meant to measure the permission cache, mixing in the new denial cache makes dashboards/alerts on cache effectiveness misleading (denial hits look like permission-cache hits, and permission-cache hits that deny look like misses). Consider a distinct counter for the denial cache or only recording permission-cache outcomes.
